title: Priority 4: Create Statewide Infrastructure to Power Local Programs
author: Michael B. Horn, Angela Jackson, Mallory Dwinal-Palisch and Danny Curtis
summary: This is the fifth of six Clayton Christensen Institute papers by Michael B. Horn, Angela Jackson, Mallory Dwinal-Palisch and Danny Curtis offering a state policy playbook for integrated education-to-career systems. It argues that because career-connected programs take shape locally, states should act as shared infrastructure that gives schools, colleges, workforce organizations and employers common information, structures and capacity. Recommendation 4.1 is to create shared data and resources, illustrated by the Colorado Workforce Development Council's Talent Pipeline Report, TalentFOUND dashboard and credential frameworks. Recommendation 4.2 is to require and support collaboration, illustrated by Louisiana's Jump Start regional partnerships, Jump Start 2.0 and Fast Forward. Recommendation 4.3 is to invest in organizations that bridge employers and education providers, illustrated by South Carolina's Apprenticeship Carolina. Each recommendation is read through Business Model Theory and a Chesterton's Fence caution against one-size-fits-all standardization, and each ends with takeaways for other states.
points: States should function as shared infrastructure, supplying labor-market analysis, employer-engagement capacity, curriculum frameworks and technical expertise that no local provider can efficiently build alone.
Colorado shows the value lies in helping institutions interpret and act on labor-market data, not simply in publishing it.
Louisiana paired a collaboration requirement for Jump Start with technical assistance, cross-agency review and later reforms when credential quality fell short.
South Carolina's Apprenticeship Carolina has helped more than 1,500 companies register programs and about 53,000 learners become registered apprentices.
Shared guidance should leave room for local judgment, and support organizations should reduce friction without taking design ownership away from employers and educators.
quotes: In this role, state policy functions as shared infrastructure that local providers can plug into as they build career-connected pathways.

Doing that work once at the state level can reduce the cost of pathway development across many communities while still leaving local partners room to respond to regional labor markets and student needs.
The goal therefore is not one-size-fits-all standardization. It is shared guidance that leaves room for local judgment.
Colorado shows that the value lies not simply in publishing labor-market information, but in helping institutions interpret and act on it.

Louisiana did not simply require schools, colleges, employers, and workforce agencies to collaborate and then leave them to it. It built the scaffolding these partnerships needed and treated implementation as an iterative process.
Louisiana’s early results showed that rapid growth in pathways and credential attainment did not necessarily mean students were earning credentials with strong labor-market or postsecondary value.
The core problem these organizations solve is that no single participant in a work-based learning or apprenticeship partnership has a business model in place to do everything such programs require.
Since its launch in 2007, the organization has helped more than 1,500 companies register apprenticeship programs and about nearly 53,000 learners become registered apprentices.
